book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook would define depreciation/devaluation, state the Marshall-Lerner logic and then draw the J-curve. Here the video starts from a felt problem (a person with no money, then a country with no foreign currency), shows how BoP deficits drain reserves into a crisis, asks 'how to stop it?', narrows eight remedies to two, writes the chain as a promise with a '?' on the key link, and only then proves the link with two mirrored stories in rupees (an export that becomes worth it, an import that becomes too dear). The J-curve comes last as a warning ('but remember, not at once'), after the learner already believes the long-run effect.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Build the whole cause chain first with an open question on its weakest link, then prove that link with one export story and one mirrored import story using the same two exchange rates, and finish with the time caveat.

narration.density: About 16 terms (financial/economic crisis, foreign currency, foreign debt obligations, BoP crisis, current account, capital account, forex reserve, BoP disequilibrium and its eight measures as one list, depreciation, devaluation, exchange rate, trade balance, competitiveness, short/long term, J-curve) in about 557 s, about 1.7 per minute. Comfortable: two long number stories (about 200 s) carry one link of the chain. The eight-measure list (176-197 s) is the one rushed spot; the J-curve reason (512-546 s) is spoken slowly but without a picture.

talmel_summary: Picture and voice are close throughout: most tiles land within 1 s of their word, and when the picture leads it is by 1-4 s, usually a number or label written just before it is said. The fit is best in the two stories, where every spoken number lands where it belongs (rate bars, struck and rewritten sums, a frame that jumps to the rate in force, bubbles that flip on the decision word, ticks that land on the chain). It is weakest where the words explain why: the J-curve dip is explained for about 30 s with only a dot moving on an unlabelled curve, and 'decreases the exchange rate' is written beside a number that goes up. No tile falls in a transcript gap.

voice.notes: About 200 recognised words per minute, warm and storytelling, slightly faster in lists. Talks to the viewer ('aap kisi se poochhenge', 'zara soch ke dekhiye', 'ek baat yaad rakhna'), gives the character a casual voice ('dekho yaar'), and slows down on rupee values (3 point 3, 4 point 7 6, 14 point 2 8). Signposts each turn ('chaliye ise ek example se samajhte hain', 'to ye to baat hui exports ki'). The textbook line on competitiveness is said with a 'isliye hum kehte hain' frame, marking it as the line to remember.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a small exporter: a product sells for Rs 10 at home and has a dollar price abroad; each year the exchange rate card changes (3.30, 4.76, ...) and the player decides 'sell at home' or 'export', and may cut the dollar price to win buyers.
game_ideas.process_happens: The rupee value of each export is computed live (price x rate); buyers abroad switch to the cheapest seller; the country's export bar and forex locker fill as exports rise.
game_ideas.win: Earn the most rupees over five years and help the forex locker out of the red zone.
game_ideas.lose: Exporting at $3 when the rate is 3.30 shows Rs 9.90 < Rs 10 (a loss against selling at home); pricing above rivals shows buyers walking to a competitor.
game_ideas.concept: export effect worked example (1948 vs 1949 rate, spice box)

game_ideas.player_does: Is the finance ministry for ten years: each year sets policy (devalue, control imports, promote exports, do nothing) while oil-import bills and debt payments arrive.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each year's BoP is added to the forex lockers (green arrow in, red arrow out); if the lockers empty, the oil tanker cannot unload and a debt notice turns red: BoP crisis.
game_ideas.win: Keep reserves above the crisis line every year while paying for oil and debt.
game_ideas.lose: Doing nothing through repeated deficits drains the lockers into the pink 'BoP crisis' zone, as in 1991.
game_ideas.concept: persistent BoP deficit drains forex into a BoP crisis (India 1991, Sri Lanka)

game_ideas.player_does: After a devaluation, steers the trade balance quarter by quarter: imports already contracted must be paid at the new rate; the player chooses when to cut imports and when exporters can ramp up.
game_ideas.process_happens: The trade balance line is drawn live: it first dips (old import contracts cost more), then rises as new export orders arrive; the J shape forms from the player's own moves.
game_ideas.win: Hold course through the dip and end above the starting trade balance.
game_ideas.lose: Reversing the devaluation in the dip locks in the losses and the curve never rises, showing why the J needs time.
game_ideas.concept: J-curve: trade balance worsens in the short term, improves in the long term

game_ideas.player_does: Drags boxes into order: devaluation -> rupee value falls (more rupees per dollar) -> exports up / imports down -> trade balance -> BoP -> forex reserves.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each correct link lights up and a small coin moves along it into the forex locker.
game_ideas.win: Complete chain with the direction words matching the rate number.
game_ideas.lose: Placing 'forex reserves rise' before 'trade balance improves', or saying the rupees-per-dollar number falls, breaks the chain and shows the contradiction.
game_ideas.concept: depreciation/devaluation -> lower exchange rate -> exports up, imports down -> trade balance -> BoP -> forex

checks_learned: Direction words must agree with the number shown: if the script says the exchange rate 'decreases' while Rs per $ rises (3.30 -> 4.76), it must say 'the rupee's value falls; more rupees per dollar'.
Every graph axis must be labelled; a curve whose vertical axis is unnamed (J-curve) fails the check.
Real people's photos and real brand logos or products are blocked; the story keeps its numbers with a generic character and product.
A year written on screen (Sri Lanka 2022) must be spoken, or the spoken 'recently' replaced by the year.
Arithmetic in story numbers is checked by code (3 x 3.30 = 9.90, 3 x 4.76 = 14.28, 2.5 x 4.76 = 11.9, 100000 x 4.76 = 4.76 lakh); all correct here, keep enforcing.
A 'why' explanation spoken for more than 20 s needs its own visual step (here imports already contracted costing more should be drawn on the J-curve dip).
Imported screenshot panels (the eight-measure list) must be redrawn as BIE drawings with readable text.
Ads or promo overlays must not cover the canvas during a recap.
When two paired terms are always shown together (depreciation, devaluation), the script should give at least one line on how they differ or flag it as a later lesson.

teaching_best.why: Opens with a person's bad times (no food money, unpaid loan) and maps them onto a country's (no money for oil, unpaid foreign debt) before naming BoP crisis.
The whole chain is shown first as a promise with a '?' on its key link, so the long stories that follow have a clear job: answer that '?'.
One running pair of rates (3.30 and 4.76) carries both an export story and a mirrored import story; each ends in a decision flip and a tick on the chain.
The what-if price cut ($2.5 still gives Rs 11.9) turns 'competitiveness' from a textbook word into a number the learner can check.
'Ek baat yaad rakhna': the J-curve is taught as a caveat after the long-run effect is believed, and the learner's 'why?' is voiced before the answer.

teaching_weak.why: 'Exchange rate decreases' is never unpacked into 'more rupees per dollar', though the stories show the number going up; learners may get the direction backwards.
The story uses a real brand and its owner's photo for invented events; BIE must use a generic character.
Eight remedies are read out as a list in about 20 s with no explanation before six are dropped.
The J-curve reason is only spoken; no import bill is shown jumping, and the curve's vertical axis is unnamed.
The difference between depreciation and devaluation is pushed to the next video, though both terms are used all through.
